transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-21 09:34 PT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Kim (Redwood AE), Miguel Alvarez (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Nimbus SRE), Priya Menon (Nimbus Head of ML), Evan Cho (Nimbus Infra)

Auto-summary: quick discovery focused on reliability and incident tolerance. Customer runs recommendation/chat in EU + US, priority is predictable latency under failures, automated fallbacks, and auditability for compliance.

[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Sarah, I'm the AE on this account, with Miguel from our systems team. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Raj Patel: Hey Sarah, good, thanks. Ready to dive in.
[00:10] Miguel Alvarez: morning all, quick agenda: understand your infra, critical failure modes, desired SLA, and then we can walk through Redwood's routing/fallback options.
[00:18] Priya Menon: sounds good. To set context, we run a real-time recommender + chat assistant on our e-com site. Bulk of traffic is EU and US east, peak 1200 RPS during flash sales, typical 200-300 RPS. Latency target is p95 sub 120ms for recommend calls and sub 200ms for chat generation.
[00:32] Evan Cho: We also have data residency constraints for EU customers and audit requirements for certain partners.
[00:38] Sarah Kim: great, thanks. Miguel, do you want to talk through the failure modes and routing patterns we typically recommend?
[00:44] Miguel Alvarez: Sure. So there are a few layers: first, regional failover requests can be routed to a nearby region and we can do automatic geo-failover based on health checks. Second, capacity-tier fallback e.g., hosted -> dedicated -> private model variants or cheaper quantized models if the premium variant is saturated. Third, model variant fallback switch to an NLG model with lower compute profile. We also support prefix/KV cache preservation for warm sessions so cold starts are minimized.
[01:05] Raj Patel: When you say geo-failover, is that automatic, and how quick is it? We can't afford long periods of degraded quality during sales.
[01:12] Miguel Alvarez: Health checks are ~10s by default, but you can configure aggressive thresholds. Most customers see DNS + routing convergence within 30-60s depending on regional DNS TTLs and circuit breakers. We also have active-request draining so in-flight requests are retried to the fallback pool.
[01:26] Priya Menon: That seems long for us; 60s is a lot in a flash sale. Do you do any client-side multiplexing or edge caching to cover it?
[01:33] Miguel Alvarez: We do a few things: prefix/KV cache on the serving layer keeps repeated prompts super-fast, and smart routing can proactively replicate hot state to a standby region. For ultra-low RTO, customers run a hybrid with Dedicated in their primary region and Hosted as a failover that reduces routing time because the fallback pool is already warmed.
[01:50] Sarah Kim: to add, for customers with strict RTO we recommend a small reserved Dedicated pool in primary region + hosted as cross-region fallback, so you get both predictability and global resilience.
[01:58] Evan Cho: ok, cost eyeball: how does that pricing look? We have to justify reserved GPU cost vs burst hosted during peaks.
[02:04] Sarah Kim: high-level, reserved capacity buys you lower per-token cost and priority scheduling; hosted is pay-as-you-go with slightly higher unit cost but infinite-ish burst. We'll share a ballpark pricing sheet after the call.
[02:12] Raj Patel: SLA-wise, what numbers do you commit? Our internal SLO is 99.95 for inference availability; we understand full 100 is impossible but we need near-prod guarantees and good incident communication.
[02:23] Miguel Alvarez: Our Dedicated offering has SLA tiers: 99.9 and 99.95 options depending on multi-AZ and reserved sizing. Hosted has best-effort public SLA for free-tier accounts, enterprise hosted contracts can get SLA add-ons. For strict 99.95+ we typically recommend Dedicated + multi-region standby.
[02:38] Priya Menon: and does the SLA cover model quality regressions if you automatically fallback to cheaper quantized models?
[02:45] Miguel Alvarez: good question SLA covers availability, not model quality. For quality-sensitive flows we use canary policies: if a fallback is triggered we can route a percentage of traffic to the variant and evaluate quality metrics. Also Redwood Optimize provides prompt set regressions and alerts if quality drops.
[02:59] Raj Patel: about caching if we have KV cache and we failover region, do we lose the cache and force cold starts?
[03:05] Miguel Alvarez: by default caches are local to the serving cluster but we do replication for hot entries between primary and standby region for customers that opt in. There's a tradeoff: replication adds small network overhead but cuts RTO.
[03:16] Priya Menon: what about stateful conversations? We need to keep session context for chat across failovers.
[03:22] Miguel Alvarez: session context can be stored in your backend and we recommend a small sticky session window with tokenized context rehydration. For very low latency you can use Redwood's prefix caching and session snapshot transfer to standby region. We'll show a reference architecture in the playbook.
[03:36] Evan Cho: security: we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs for data egress and model inference. Also SSO for RBAC.
[03:43] Sarah Kim: we integrate with customer KMS; we support AWS KMS and HSM partners in private deployments, full audit logs and token-level tracing available in Redwood Console, and SAML SSO + SCIM for user provisioning.
[03:53] Raj Patel: is Private deployment an option for us? We might need VPC or on-prem for certain EU customers.
[03:58] Miguel Alvarez: yes, Redwood Private runs in your VPC or on-prem; it gives you full control over networking, keys, and audit retention. The tradeoff is we manage the control plane (optionally) but compute can be customer-managed. For strict regulatory needs we do air-gapped installs too.
[04:11] Priya Menon: ok timeline: we want to run a 2-week POC that verifies latency under failover, measures cold-start frequency, and validates quality regression when using quantized fallbacks. Can Redwood support that?
[04:20] Miguel Alvarez: absolutely. Typical POC: ingest sample traffic, run baseline on your current infra, then route traffic through Redwood hosted + a small dedicated pool, and run a stress window to exercise failovers. We'll provide a POC plan and dashboard for token-level latency and failure classification.
[04:35] Sarah Kim: what are your success criteria? Priya?
[04:38] Priya Menon: p95 <= 120ms for recommend and p95 <= 250ms for chat during normal load; during failover we accept p95 up to 400ms but want no more than 2% error rate and no data loss.
[04:50] Raj Patel: and we want demonstrable audit trails for any inference used in regulated partners.
[04:55] Miguel Alvarez: understood. We'll include audit log retention and how to pull per-request traces in the playbook.
[05:01] Evan Cho: one more operational question: how are incidents communicated? We need on-call escalation and RCA timelines.
[05:07] Sarah Kim: for enterprise contracts we provide 24/7 support with pager escalation, SLA-backed response times, and a post-incident RCA within 72 hours for sev1 incidents.
[05:16] Priya Menon: any known gotchas? We've heard from other vendors about KV cache invalidation and cache stampedes when traffic shifts regions.
[05:23] Miguel Alvarez: yep, those are common. We recommend staggered TTLs, proactive warm-up, and circuit breakers on the client. Redwood's runtime also supports per-key backoff so you don't get thundering herd if a cache miss hits.
[05:36] Raj Patel: curious, can you show us an example of routing policy config? Is it declarative, and can we tie it to our internal SLOs?
[05:43] Miguel Alvarez: it's declarative via the config API and Console. You can define priorities (region, cost-tier, model-variant), health check thresholds, and fallback windows. We also emit SLO metrics that can be ingested into your monitoring. We'll include a sample policy in the playbook.
[05:57] Sarah Kim: ok let's recap next steps and owners. We'll send the reliability playbook & multi-region doc, Miguel will run baseline benchmarks, Priya will share sample traffic and success criteria, and we'll aim to kick off the POC week of Aug 2. Anyone disagree?
[06:10] Priya Menon: sounds good.
[06:12] Raj Patel: yep thanks.
[06:14] Sarah Kim: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
